issues.legal_issue: A governmental takeover of a religious shrine’s management for temporary administrative purposes does not extinguish the lawful manager’s title when the takeover order does not purport to do so.
material_facts: The Mahant asked the government to take over management of the shrine amid disputes and allegations of mismanagement.
The government took over administration and approved a recommendation that management remain under its control until specified circumstances improved.
The orders addressed management of the shrine and its properties; they did not state that the Mahant’s title to manage them was extinguished.
issues.conclusion: The takeover orders were executive and temporary in character and did not extinguish the Mahant’s title to manage the shrine and its properties.
issues.legal_principle: Section 30 of the Gwalior State Places of Worship and Religious Endowments Aid and Administration Act, 1930, empowered the government in specified circumstances to take over management. The orders here exercised that administrative power; they were not legislative acts extinguishing the Mahant’s title. Although the sovereign could have extinguished that title, the orders did not do so. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.appeal_against_restoration_decree: A government appeals from a decree restoring management of religious property to the person entitled to manage it.
predicates.government_takeover_for_management: The government takes control of property to manage it after the manager requests assistance or administrative concerns arise.
predicates.order_does_not_extinguish_title: The order taking control does not state that the lawful manager’s title is extinguished.
predicates.lawful_manager_title_survives: The lawful manager’s title to manage the property remains in force.

issues.definition: When a government appeals a restoration decree after taking control only for management under an order that does not extinguish title, the manager’s title remains in force.

issues.legal_issue: After the Constitution takes effect, the State cannot continue to withhold management of property from the person entitled to manage it without lawful authority.
material_facts: The Mahant sought restoration of the shrine’s management after the disputes had ended.
The State continued to retain management of the shrine and its properties.
The Mahant’s title to manage the property had not been extinguished, and the State identified no lawful authority for retaining management after the Constitution took effect.
issues.conclusion: The State had no competence to withhold management from the Mahant after the Constitution took effect without authority of law, and the Mahant was entitled to restoration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 30 of the Gwalior Act authorized the government to take over management in specified circumstances, but the Act did not authorize continued retention against the lawful manager after the Constitution took effect. The absence of a statutory process for releasing property under government management did not bar the lawful manager from claiming it; an outstanding title could be defeated only under lawful authority. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: claim_for_restoration_of_management and claimant_has_outstanding_management_title and state_retains_management_after_constitution and no_law_authorizes_retention

predicates.claim_for_restoration_of_management: A person brings a claim seeking restoration of management of property held by the State.
predicates.claimant_has_outstanding_management_titl: The claimant has a lawful title to manage the property that has not been extinguished.
predicates.state_retains_management_after_constitut: The State continues to hold management of the property after the Constitution takes effect.
predicates.no_law_authorizes_retention: No law authorizes the State to continue withholding management from the lawful manager.
predicates.state_must_restore_management: The State must restore management to the person entitled to manage the property.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks restoration, retains an unextinguished management title, and the State continues management after the Constitution takes effect without legal authority, the State must restore management.

issues.legal_issue: A government’s takeover of property solely for management does not establish adverse possession when it makes no claim hostile to the lawful manager’s rights.
material_facts: The State took over the shrine and its properties for management.
The State did not purport to claim an interest adverse to the Mahant’s right to manage the property.
The State relied on its management of the property as a defence of adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by adverse possession because the government had taken over the property only for management and had made no adverse claim against the Mahant.
issues.legal_principle: Possession taken for management, without a claim adverse to the lawful manager’s rights, does not amount to adverse possession. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.claim_to_recover_property: A person brings a claim to recover property held by the government.
predicates.government_possession_only_for_managemen: The government holds the property only to administer or manage it.
predicates.no_hostile_claim_against_manager: The government has not asserted an interest hostile to the lawful manager’s rights.
predicates.adverse_possession_does_not_bar_claim: The claim is not barred by adverse possession.

issues.definition: When a recovery claim concerns property held only for management and the government has made no hostile claim against the manager, adverse possession does not bar the claim.
